So it was revealed: ﴿Yes, [We will]﴾ (75:4), which made obligatory what follows the negation, namely the gathering, so it is as if it was said: "Yes, We will gather them."

It was read *qādirūn* ("we are capable"), i.e., "We are capable."

It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him: he advances the sin and postpones repentance. He says: "I will repent, I will repent," until death comes upon him in the worst of his conditions and his most evil of deeds.

(ʿ).] It has also been said: it is the soul that blames itself that day for neglecting increase if it was virtuous, and for negligence if it was sinful. The answer to the oath is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ (75:3), and it is: "You will surely be resurrected." Qatada read *an lan najmaʿa ʿiẓāmahu* in the passive voice. The meaning is: We will assemble them after their dispersal, after they have become decayed and crumbled, mixed with dust, after the winds have scattered them and carried them to remote lands. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed him, and he said: "Even if I witnessed that day, I would not believe you, O Muhammad, nor have faith in it, unless Allah gathers the bones." So it was revealed: ﴿Yes, [We will]﴾ (75:4), which made obligatory what follows the negation, namely the gathering, so it is as if it was said: "Yes, We will gather them."

﴿Capable﴾ is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in *najmaʿ* (we gather): i.e., We gather the bones, being capable of assembling all of them and restoring them to their original form, until We make even his fingertips level, meaning his fingers, which are the extremities and the last part by which his creation is completed. ﴿But man desires﴾ (75:5) is a conjunction onto *ayaḥsabu* (does he think). ﴿Barita al-basar﴾ (the eye was dazzled): it was bewildered and dismayed by fear. Its origin is from *barija al-rajul* (a man was dazzled), when he looked at lightning and his sight was stunned.

It is also read as *baraqa* ("shone"), from *al-bariq* (glittering), meaning that it gleamed because of the intensity of its fixed staring.

Abu al-Sammal read *baliqa*, meaning it opened and widened. It is said: *balaqa al-bāb*, *ablaqahu* and *ballaqahu*, meaning he opened the door.

﴿Wa-khasafa al-qamar﴾ (the moon was eclipsed): its light vanished, or it vanished itself.

It is read *wa-khusifa* in the passive form.

﴿Wa-jumi'a al-shams wa-al-qamar﴾ (the sun and the moon will be joined together): where God causes them to rise from the west. It was said: they will be joined in the loss of light. It was also said: they will be brought together as two black, rolled-up bodies, as if they were two slaughtered bulls (*thawrān 'aqīrān*) in the fire. It was said: they will be brought together and then hurled into the sea, and this will be the great fire of God.

﴿Al-mafarr﴾ (the place of escape): with a fatha on the first letter it is the verbal noun (*al-maṣdar*), and with a kasra it is the place. It may also be a verbal noun like *al-marji'* (the return). It is read with both vowels.

﴿Kallā﴾ (No!) is a deterrent from seeking escape.

﴿Lā wazar﴾ (there is no refuge): no shelter. Whatever you take refuge in, whether a mountain or something else, and are saved by, is your *wizr* (refuge).

﴿Ilā rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr﴾ (To your Lord alone, on that day, is the place of settling): the settling place of the servants, meaning their settling. The sense is that they cannot settle down with anyone else or turn to anyone else. [Editor's note: in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *naṣaba al-qawm* means the people travelled through their day at a gentle pace, and *naṣiba al-rajul* (with a kasra) means he became weary.] Or it means: to His judgment the affairs of the servants return, and none other judges in them, as in His saying: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾ (40:16). Or it means: to your Lord is their *mustaqarr*, the place of their dwelling, whether Paradise or Hell. That is, He entrusts this to His will: whomever He wills He admits to Paradise, and whomever He wills He admits to Hell.

﴿Bimā qaddama﴾ (by what he sent forward): of deeds he did.

﴿Wa-bimā akhkhara﴾ (and what he left behind): of deeds he did not do; or of his wealth, what he gave in charity; or what he left behind and his heirs inherited. It is said: by what he sent forward of good or evil deeds, and what he left behind of good or evil practice, by which others acted after him. It is related from Mujahid: by the first of his deeds and the last of them. A similar verse is: ﴿He will inform them of what they did; God has counted it, and they have forgotten it﴾ (58:6).

﴿Baṣīrah﴾ (a clear insight): a clear proof, described as "seeing" by figurative usage (*majāz*), just as the verses are described as "seeing" in His saying: ﴿When Our signs came to them as clear sight﴾ (27:13). Or it means: an eye that sees. The meaning is that he will be informed of his deeds even if he is not informed, so there is in it what suffices instead of informing, because it (the man) is a witness against himself through what he did, since his limbs speak of it: ﴿On the day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ (24:24).

﴿Wa-law alqā ma'ādhīrahu﴾ (even if he presents his excuses): even if he brings every excuse with which he defends himself and argues on its behalf. It is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: even if he let down his curtains. He said: *al-ma'ādhīr* are curtains, and its singular is *ma'dhār*. If this is sound, it is because it prevents seeing the one who is veiled, just as an excuse prevents the punishment of the sinner. If you ask: Should not the analogical plural of *ma'dhira* be *ma'āthir* rather than *ma'ādhīr*? I answer: *ma'ādhīr* is not the plural of *ma'dhira*; it is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) for it, similar to *al-manākīr* for *al-munkar*.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 75, verses 16–25:**

The pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ (*bihi*, "with it") refers to the Qur'an.

When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) received the revelation, he would compete with Jibril (Gabriel) in reciting it. He did not wait until Jibril had finished, out of eagerness to memorize and fear that it would slip from him. So he was commanded to listen attentively, directing his heart and hearing toward it, until its revelation was completed for him. Then he would follow it with study until it became firmly fixed in him. The meaning is: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ by reciting the revelation while Jibril, may the blessings of God be upon him, is reciting, ﴿so that you may hasten with it﴾, that is, take it in haste, and lest it slip away from you.

Then he gave the reason for the prohibition of haste in His words: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection﴾ in your breast and the establishing of its recitation on your tongue. ﴿So when We have recited it﴾, He made Jibril's recitation His own recitation. The word *al-Qur'an* means "the recitation." ﴿Then follow its recitation﴾, that is, be attentive to it and do not compete with its reciter. Accept within yourself that it will not remain unmemorized, for We guarantee its preservation for you. ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation﴾, should anything in its meanings become unclear to you. It was as if he were hastening both in memorizing and in asking about its meaning together, as you see some who are eager for knowledge do.

﴿Do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾. The words ﴿No!﴾ are a restraint upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the habit of haste and a rebuke for it, and an exhortation to deliberateness and patience. He emphasized this by following it with His words: ﴿Rather, you love the hasty life﴾. It is as if He said: "Rather, you, O children of Adam, because you were created of haste and were made to be hasty, hasten in everything. For this reason you love the hasty life and ﴿leave the Hereafter﴾." It has also been read with the *ya'* (you-plural third-person form, *yadharuna* / *yuhibbuna* style), and this is more emphatic.

If you ask: how is His saying ﴿Do not move your tongue with it﴾ and what follows connected to the mention of the Resurrection? I answer: its connection to it is through this: it is a transition from it to the rebuke for loving the hasty life and neglecting concern for the Hereafter.

**The face (al-wajh):** an expression for the whole (*al-jumla*) of the person.

[Mahmud said: "The faces are a metonymy for the whole person, and He placed ﴿to its Lord﴾ first to convey restriction (*al-hasr*) ... etc."

Ahmad said: How short his tongue falls at this verse! How often he hums and drones on denying the vision, splitting the cloak and multiplying and going to extremes! But when this verse opened his mouth, he [the Mu'tazilite] had to contend with it by argument, saying that if the intended meaning were vision, it would not be restricted by placing the object first, because in that case it would not be restricted to the vision of God Most High. He does not realize that one who enjoys seeing the beauty of God's face does not turn his gaze away from it, does not prefer anything over it, and does not look at anything other than it, and it is fitting that he restrict his seeing to the One about whom ﴿there is nothing like Him﴾. We see the lover in this world: when he is granted sight of his beloved, he does not turn his glance away or prefer anything over it. How much more so for the one who loves God, Mighty and Majestic, when the gaze upon His noble face is granted to him! We ask the Mighty God not to turn His face away from us, and to protect us from the slippery paths of innovation and the pitfalls of doubt. He is our sufficiency and the best Disposer of affairs.]

**"Radiant" (al-nadira):** from the radiance (*nadrat*) of bliss. ﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾, looking at their Lord exclusively and not looking at anything else. This is the meaning of placing the object first.

Do you not see His saying: ﴿To your Lord, that Day, is the place of rest﴾; ﴿To your Lord, that Day, is the driving﴾; ﴿To God the matter returns﴾; ﴿And to God is the final return﴾; ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾; ﴿Upon Him I have relied and to Him I turn back﴾. How the placing [of the object] here indicates the meaning of exclusivity! And it is known that they look at things that cannot be encompassed by restriction nor enter under number, in a gathering where all creation assembles. The believers are the beholders of that day, because they are the secure, on whom there is no fear and who do not grieve. So their looking at Him exclusively, if He were something seen, would be impossible. Therefore it is necessary to interpret it as a meaning with which exclusivity is valid.

[The words "if He were something seen" — the non-visibility of God is based on the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, which is the impermissibility of seeing Him. The doctrine of the People of the Sunna is that it is permissible. It is possible that the placing of the object here is for emphasis on mentioning the one looked at, which requires the radiance of the faces of the beholders, not for exclusivity. (Ibn ʿAtiyya? [ʿ])]

With which exclusivity is valid is what people say: "I am looking toward so-and-so, to see what he will do with me," meaning expectation and hope. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"And when I look to you, O king, [while the sea lies beyond you], you increase my blessings."*

He says: when I hope for your noble qualities, you increase my blessings, so looking toward him is a metonymy for that. It is also possible that the meaning is: by merely my looking toward you, you respond to me beyond my request, without needing to state the request explicitly. "From a king" is a specifying *tamyiz* accompanied by *min*. "The sea lies beyond you" is a parenthetical or circumstantial clause, meaning: you are less than the one who is greater than you in goodness and nobility.

I heard a beggar's begging poem in Mecca at noon, when people close their doors and retire to their rest. He says:

*"[Your] ʿuyayna ... and a glance toward God and toward you."*

The meaning is that they expect blessing and honor only from their Lord, just as in this world they feared and hoped for none but Him.

**"Scowling" (bāsira):** one who is very stern in frowning. **"Brave" (bāsil):** more intense than that, but the word has come to be used for the courageous when his frown is severe.

﴿Thinking﴾: expecting that something will be done to them of a kind that is, in its severity and dreadfulness, ﴿a calamity﴾, a disaster that breaks the spine, just as the radiant faces expected that every good would be done to them.

The pronoun in "balaghat" (﴿when it reaches﴾) refers to the soul (al-nafs), though no mention of it has preceded, because the speech in which it occurs indicates it, as Hatim said:

Amawiyya, what good is wealth to a man
when he is gurgling one day and his chest is constricted.
Amawiyya, indeed wealth goes and comes,
and what remains of wealth is talk and remembrance.
People know well that if Hatim
wished for the abundance of wealth, he would have it in plenty.

(These lines are by Hatim al-Ta'i. The hamza is for the vocative, and "Mawa" is a diminutive (murakhkham), its original form being "Mawiyya," the name of his mother, who was the daughter of Ufayr, and she used to blame him. Its origin is a reference to water, because she resembles it in softness, delicacy, clarity and abundance. "Al-thurwa" means wealth. "Al-hashraja" is the rattling of the breath's sound in the chest. The pronoun refers to the soul, though it has not been mentioned, by claim, because of its fame. It is narrated that when Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was on his deathbed, A'isha said to him, "By your life, what good is..." the verse, and he said: "Do not say this, my daughter." ﴿And the agony of death came with truth﴾, and this is a reading attributed to him. He repeated the call "Mawiyya" as a reproach. "Ghad" and "ra'ih" mean one who comes and one who goes. His saying "min al-mal" means "from its effects." If "'alima" were to be detached from acting on the object and he expressed himself with the apparent noun, that is because this speech is spoken by the souls of people, so its issuing from them is taken into account.

"Thara'uhu al-mal" means being rich by it, or gathering it. "Al-wafr" means increase and abundant wealth.)

The Arabs say, "arsalat," meaning "the rain came," and you can hardly hear them mention the sky. ﴿The collarbones﴾, the bones surrounding the notch of the throat on the right and left. He mentions the difficulty of death, which is the first stage of the Hereafter, when the soul reaches the collarbones and its departure draws near.
